summary: Changes the type codes and mnemonics of the DNSSEC records SIG, KEY and NXT to avoid dangerous interactions between older resolvers and servers that understand the new delegation signer semantics. One failure case made an unsecured zone unresolvable. It updates RFC 2535 and RFC 3658, and was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC had changed the meaning of one of its record types without changing the type number, and old resolvers read the new meaning the wrong way. That made a zone with an unsigned delegation look like it did not exist. This RFC gives the three affected record types new numbers and new names, so an old resolver treats them as records it does not recognise and moves on.

questions: why were dnssec sig key nxt records renamed
what is the difference between nxt and nsec
what are the dnssec rrsig nsec and dnskey type codes
why did ds break legacy resolvers
subtitle: Renaming three DNSSEC record types so that old resolvers ignore them instead of misreading them.

tldr.problem: Adding the Delegation Signer record gave the NXT record new meaning, and widely deployed resolvers that follow RFC 2535 treat any answer containing an NXT as proof that the requested name does not exist. A zone with an unsigned delegation could then become impossible to resolve.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives SIG, KEY and NXT new type codes and new names, RRSIG, DNSKEY and NSEC. A resolver that does not know the new codes sees unknown records and skips them, so the old behaviour cannot be triggered.
tldr.outcome: Signing a zone no longer breaks the zones it delegates to, which removes the main obstacle to deploying DNSSEC. RFC 3755 was obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

today: RFC 3755 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, and it was updated by RFC 3757 and RFC 3845.

sections.title: The Problem with NXT and DS
sections.content:
DNSSEC had been through many iterations whose syntax and semantics are not completely compatible, as part of the ordinary process of proposing a protocol, implementing it, testing it in a diverse environment and refining the definitions. The DNSSEC process was complicated by the criticality and wide deployment of DNS, and by the need to add security while minimising daily operational complexity.

One weak area of earlier DNS specifications was the lack of detail about resolver behaviour, which left implementors to decide many details themselves. Combined with the number of iterations DNSSEC had been through, this produced deployed code with a wide variety of behaviours, and made it hard to predict how a protocol change would be handled by every resolver in the field.

The specific problem came from Delegation Signer's introduction of new semantics for the NXT record that are incompatible with RFC 2535. In RFC 2535, NXT records were only required to be returned as part of a non-existence proof. With DS, an unsecure referral returns, in addition to the NS record, a proof that no DS record exists, in the form of an NXT and a SIG over that NXT. RFC 2535 did not say how a resolver should interpret a response with RCODE=0, AA=0, and both an NS and an NXT in the authority section. Some widely deployed RFC 2535 aware resolvers interpret any answer with an NXT as a proof that the requested record does not exist, which makes unsecure delegations invisible to them and breaks the principle that DNSSEC must do no harm, since signing a zone must not prevent the resolution of unsecured delegations.

The RFC defines an unsecure delegation as any delegation for which no DS record appears at the parent, and an unsecure referral as an answer from the parent containing an NS RRset and a proof that no DS record exists for that name.
sections.plainLanguage: The trouble started when DNSSEC gave the NXT record a second job. Under the old rules, NXT appeared only to prove that a name does not exist. With the Delegation Signer record, a server also sends NXT to prove that the parent does not vouch for the child zone. Many resolvers in the field read any NXT as proof of non-existence, so they concluded the child zone did not exist at all.

sections.title: The Alternatives Considered
sections.content:
The RFC sets out several ways to keep legacy resolvers from seeing the new semantics, and explains why each was or was not chosen.

Changing the type codes for SIG, KEY and NXT is the simplest way to hide unsecure referrals from legacy resolvers. The drawback is that new resolvers cannot validate zones signed with the old records, but that problem already exists because of the changes made by DS, and resolvers that understand the old records are far more prevalent than zones signed under RFC 2535.

Changing only the NXT type code, or a subset that includes it, has the appearance of simplicity, but it risks new problems and may not go far enough, since more incompatibilities may exist between DS and earlier semantics. Legacy resolvers may also be confused by seeing records they recognise, SIG and KEY, while being unable to find NXT. Changing all the type codes at once leaves legacy resolvers and tools completely blinded to DNSSEC, so they see only unknown records.

Two other approaches rely on EDNS0. Assigning a new flag bit to signal DS-awareness, tentatively called DA, and having authoritative servers send DNSSEC data only in response to queries with that bit set, would work only if every legacy resolver zeroes out EDNS0 flags it does not understand. Since it is impractical to know how every implementation handles unknown flags, this is not a universal solution, though it could be used in addition to changing the type codes. Incrementing the EDNS version number assumes that all existing implementations reject higher versions than they support, and that approach has not been tested.

Doing nothing was the last option. As long as a large deployed base of resolvers interprets any answer with an NXT as a non-existence proof, zone owners have a strong incentive not to sign zones that contain unsecure delegations, which would slow DNSSEC adoption sharply. Without signed zones there is no clear incentive for resolver operators to upgrade, and historical data suggests resolvers are rarely upgraded and old nameserver code never dies. A protocol change removes the disincentive immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: Four options were considered. Renaming all three record types hides the new behaviour from old resolvers, but old resolvers can no longer check old signatures. Changing only one type code leaves the others visible and may miss other clashes. Marking DNSSEC awareness with a new EDNS0 flag only works if every resolver strips flags it does not recognise, which nobody can check. Doing nothing is the worst option, because zone owners will then refuse to sign anything, and nothing improves.

sections.title: The Protocol Changes
sections.content:
This document changes the type codes of SIG, KEY and NXT. The RFC calls this the cleanest and safest of the options, largely because the behaviour of resolvers that receive unknown type codes is well understood, and because it has received the most testing.

The mnemonics change as well, to avoid operational confusion. DNSKEY replaces KEY, with the mnemonic indicating that these keys are not for application use. RRSIG, for Resource Record SIGnature, replaces SIG, and NSEC, for Next SECure, replaces NXT. These new types completely replace the old ones, except that SIG(0) and TKEY continue to use SIG and KEY.

The new types have exactly the same syntax and semantics as SIG, KEY and NXT in RFC 2535 and RFC 3658, with three exceptions. Domain names embedded in RRSIG and NSEC records MUST NOT be compressed. Embedded domain names in RRSIG and NSEC records are not downcased for DNSSEC canonical form and ordering, nor for equality comparison. An RRSIG with a type-covered field of zero has undefined semantics, and the meaning of such a record may only be defined by IETF Standards Action.

A resolver that receives the old types SHOULD treat them as unknown records, SHOULD NOT assign them any special meaning or treatment, and MUST NOT use them for DNSSEC validations or other DNS operational decision making. For example, a resolver MUST NOT use DNSKEYs to validate SIGs or use KEYs to validate RRSIGs. If SIG, KEY or NXT records are included in a zone they MUST NOT receive special treatment, so a SIG in a signed zone MUST have an RRSIG for it. Authoritative servers may wish to give error messages when loading zones that contain SIG or NXT records, since KEY records may still be included for SIG(0) or TKEY.

As a clarification to previous documents, some positive responses, particularly wildcard proofs and unsecure referrals, will contain NSEC records, and resolvers MUST NOT treat answers with NSEC records as negative answers merely because they contain an NSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is to give the three record types new numbers and new names: DNSKEY for KEY, RRSIG for SIG and NSEC for NXT. A resolver that predates the change sees records it does not recognise and ignores them, which stops the wrong interpretation. The RFC is strict about this: a resolver must not use the old records for any check, and it must not read an NSEC on its own as proof that a name is missing.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The IANA registry for DNS resource record types is updated by assigning types 46, 47 and 48 to RRSIG, NSEC and DNSKEY. Types 24 and 25, SIG and KEY, are retained for SIG(0) and TKEY use only, and type 30, NXT, should be marked as Obsolete.

The DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry is modified to include the applicability of each algorithm. Two new columns are added showing whether an algorithm may be used for zone signing, for transaction security mechanisms, or for both. Only algorithms usable for zone signing may be used in DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records, and only algorithms usable for SIG(0) and TSIG may be used in SIG and KEY records. All currently defined algorithms except Indirect, algorithm 252, remain usable for transaction security mechanisms. Only RSA/SHA-1, DSA/SHA-1 and the private algorithm types 253 and 254 may be used for zone signing. The registry does not carry the requirement level of each algorithm, only its applicability, so RSA/MD5 is allowed for transaction security but is NOT RECOMMENDED. This document assigns RSA/SHA-1 the presentation mnemonic RSASHA1.

A new registry is created for the DNSKEY flags field, which contains a 16-bit flags field like the KEY record. Initially it holds only bit 7, the ZONE bit; bits 0 to 6 and 8 to 15 are available for assignment. The DNSKEY protocol field is eight bits wide and its only defined value is 3, for DNSSEC, so no registry is needed for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The new records are given type codes 46, 47 and 48. The old codes for SIG and KEY are kept for the two transaction security mechanisms that still need them, and the old NXT code is retired. The algorithm registry gains a column saying where each algorithm may be used, so an algorithm approved for signing a zone cannot also be used for transaction security, and the other way round.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The changes introduced here do not materially affect security. The implications of trying to use the new and the legacy types together are not well understood, and attempts to do so would probably lead to unintended and dangerous results.

Changing type codes will leave code paths in legacy resolvers that are never exercised. Unexercised code paths are a frequent source of security holes, largely because they do not get frequent scrutiny.

Doing nothing, as described in Section 2.5, will slow DNSSEC deployment. While this does not decrease security, it also fails to increase it.
sections.plainLanguage: The change itself does not weaken security. The one risk it leaves is that old resolvers keep code for handling the old record types that can now never run, and untested code is where security holes tend to hide. Waiting instead would leave everything as it is, which protects nothing and improves nothing.

messages.label: QUERY
messages.note: The resolver asks for a name under a delegation the parent does not vouch for.

messages.label: UNSECURE REFERRAL
messages.note: The answer carries the NS record and an NXT proving that no DS record exists.

messages.label: TREATED AS NON-EXISTENCE
messages.note: The resolver reads any NXT as proof the name does not exist, so the delegation disappears.

items.title: Record types
items.text: RRSIG is 46, NSEC is 47 and DNSKEY is 48. SIG and KEY keep codes 24 and 25 for SIG(0) and TKEY, and NXT, code 30, becomes Obsolete.

items.title: Algorithm numbers
items.text: The registry now says whether an algorithm may be used for zone signing, for transaction security, or for both.

items.title: DNSKEY flags
items.text: A new 16-bit registry with only bit 7, the ZONE bit, assigned.

items.title: DNSKEY protocol
items.text: An eight bit field whose only defined value is 3, for DNSSEC.
